Considering the sheer volume of data, the Cube appears to be a library. But even with tricoders, it is impossible to read any of the passages entirely, as the holes extend far into the rock beyond your best scanning devices' reach. Even so, there's plenty to wrap one's head around, and your scientists document as much as they can.

A colossal, awe-inspiring figure towers above the ship. It looks like a giant apparition that should disappear in the blink of an eye. Impossible, too enormous to be true. And yet it refuses to dissipate like a mirage; and yet it stands.

The statue stands on a pillar, carved from the crown of a naturally formed rock, and holds a trident. It is hollow inside, and the inner walls are covered in Primordial writing. Up above, somewhere at the chest level of the statue, a stone stele hovers in the air, indifferent to gravity. It is adorned with scars from erosion, moss, and two panels with abraded, almost erased, symbols of Primordial origin.
Don't touch the stele. Have your team study the writing and learn more about this statue's purpose.

The writing primarily focuses on the topic of the hero's journey. It also includes a few myths and stories from various cultures, including those from your home planet, Earth. In addition, all those carefully carved letters contain dormant circuitry of unknown purpose. Is this statue not just a giant art piece but something more: a machine?      Then, when your people have completed their examination of the writing and raise their heads to look at the stele, it is gone.
One of the panels can be roughly translated as "courage."

Upon touching the panel, the word suddenly pulses with a glow. And so does every sentence carved on the inner walls of this statue, every single word glows except for the one from another panel on the stele — the one you didn't choose.       A vibration passes through the colossus, blowing the clouds of dust off the forgotten stone. And then, the glow fades, and silence returns. In that silence, a foreboding feeling of change, of something on the horizon, of something coming this way, begins to haunt every crew member of BCEV-07M.
One of the panels can be roughly translated as "intuition" or "foresight."

Upon touching the panel, the word suddenly pulses with a glow. And so does every sentence carved on the inner walls of this statue, every single word glows except for the one from another panel on the stele — the one you didn't choose.       A vibration passes through the colossus, blowing the clouds of dust off the forgotten stone. And then, the glow fades, and silence returns. In that silence, a foreboding feeling of change, of something on the horizon, of something coming this way, begins to haunt every crew member of BCEV-07M.

A tall rocky pillar rises from the sea, covered in long green drapes of dense vines that spread like tentacles in the water around the stone. You could almost confuse it with a giant squid about to jump out of the water.

The scouts report that this rock pillar is not a visible part of some larger underwater ridge. It does not stand on anything: it floats! And it does not sink despite its density and size. While it is not the strangest occurrence on Keeling, where you've already seen flying islands, this particular case does not appear to be related to a gravity anomaly. Instead, the secret of buoyancy lies within the lush greenery wrapped around the rock.
Send the team to carefully extract samples from the plant.

The vines are clearly parasitic: their tendrils penetrate the rock and spread throughout. After closer examination, the crew discovers that the plant is bloated with self-produced gas and a host of spores. By entering the rock and spreading, filling it with gaseous offshoots, the vines work like a giant airbag.       The scouts also report that the plant is edible, and harvest a few samples.
Have your team focus on the pillar, drilling and mining it for resources.

As your team mines the rock for resources, they are continually amazed by how far the plant's tendrils extend into the stone. And there is the answer to how the pillar floats: the plant is bloated with self-produced gas. By entering the rock and spreading around, filling it with gaseous offshoots, the vines work like a giant airbag.
Chemically decompose the plant for scientific purposes and to extract anything of value.

The vines are clearly parasitic: their tendrils penetrate the rock and spread throughout. After closer examination, the crew discovers that the plant is bloated with self-produced gas and a host of spores. By entering the rock and spreading, filling it with gaseous offshoots, the vines work like a giant airbag.       The chemical analysis shows that the plant is largely edible.
In the waters, forcefully distilled on impact, rests a large fragment of Zephyrus.

A dark rainbow of spilled fuel spreads around the wreckage. The scouts find the source of the leakage in an automated section that produced extractors. With the right materials, your crew can build new extractors from the available scrap or save some of the fuel before it is drained into the ocean.      Or you can have your crew focus on investigating this extractor-production chain and learn from its design.
Send engineers to study the fragment (its structure, design, and function) to implement this knowledge as a basis for BCEV-07M's upgrade.
The R&D lab has a few ideas on how to implement the newly acquired knowledge for the benefit of the ship.
Resource extractors were developed in this section of the ship. You can finish what was started here.
Your people put together several extractors from the components available within the wreckage.
The fuel is washed away into the ocean. What a waste!—you can find a better use for it than fish poison.
Your people create new containers for the fuel and fill them with what has not yet escaped into the ocean.
Another fragment of Zephyrus, compelled by gravity, has ended up in the waters of Keeling.
The scouts find a number of smashed escape pods within the wreckage. It seems to have been a part of one of the emergency bays.
Send engineers to study the fragment (its structure, design, and function) to implement this knowledge as a basis for BCEV-07M's upgrade.
The R&D lab has a few ideas on how to implement the newly acquired knowledge for the benefit of the ship.
The escape pods are inoperable and beyond salvation, but separate parts can be salvaged.
Your people return with a rich haul of useful items.
All escape pods are fitted with the equipment required for survival and navigation. Some of those items can be fixed.
Your people return with a rich haul of useful items.
This is the penultimate destination of another fragment of Zephyrus, before it sinks to the bottom of the ocean.

The scouts infiltrate the ruined section of Zephyrus and find an automated food production chain. Strangely enough, this section has withstood all the damage and managed to preserve a certain level of integrity, so much so that your crew believes they can fix the production chain and get a few crates of supplies made. Alternatively, you can try to save food components that haven't gone stale yet.      Or you can have your people focus on investigating this food production chain and learn from its design.
Send engineers to study the fragment (its structure, design, and function) to implement this knowledge as a basis for BCEV-07M's upgrade.
The R&D lab has a few ideas on how to implement the newly acquired knowledge for the benefit of the ship.
The automated food production chain specializes in assembling nutritious meals. You can temporarily make it work and get your dinner.
The crew nostalgically commends the last meal of Zephyrus, claiming it tastes better than the same thing cooked on the ship.
You can extract food supplies from the cooking machinery and store them on the ship.
The galley receives the final delivery of food from Zephyrus.
Flotsam from space: another piece of Zephyrus is in the vicinity of your ship.

The scouts reach the fragment and find two promising sections where something useful could have survived the landing. There is a rather well-preserved section currently on lockdown. To override the lockdown, you must power up the AI control unit and give the necessary command. Another section has detached and sunk, but your people can make an improvised diving bell to reach it.      Alternatively, a quick basic search of the easily accessible zones of the fallen fragment with scanners might be rewarding just as much as any of the other options.
Have your scouts do a quick, superficial scan of the area to see if they can find something easily available.
The scouts find a bunch of medical supplies during their search.
Have your scouts create a diving bell and reach the already sunken fragment of Zephyrus.
The scouts retrieve a rich haul from the ocean bottom.
Have your scouts get into the section on lockdown.
The AI recognizes your people and unlocks the section with all its valuables for them.
Your ship comes across one of many pieces of Zephyrus.
The fragment is large and, after so much damage, twisted and confusing. It will take time to examine the entire thing, but who knows what souvenirs can be found there.
The scouts find a battered automated medical dispenser. If fixed, it might give up some of the meds it contains.
The dispenser does the only thing it knows. It dispenses the meds to your people, and many lives might be saved now.
Equip the scouts with sensors arrays and have them thoroughly investigate this fragment.

The crooked hallways full of debris and destruction occasionally surprise with the remains of people. And it is not the bodies or gore, but personal items and trinkets that remind just how many once walked these hallways.      The scouts have to ignore these reminders and focus on the mission, retrieving a number of undamaged goods.
The scouts have found and gathered a collection of damaged goods that can be repaired if the right materials are available.
The scouts bring the mended equipment to the ship.
A tragic fragment of Zephyrus shows up from the water, for now resisting the call of the deep and staying afloat.

The scouts find one of many cracks within the ruined spaceship's hull and enter the structure.       They find the remains of a reserve reactor and a section of Zephyrus protected by the working AI control unit and alarm system, which are not friendly to anyone without a necessary clearance level. Mnemosyne claims that there should have been an experimental lab nearby, but apparently, it broke off and sank prior to your arrival.
The lab is deep enough to require a diving bell. Moreover, the ship's systems detect anomalous thermal readings. For the scouts to be safe down there, you need a reinforced diving bell.
The tech voxel transforms itself into a diving bell, able to withstand both the pressure and any prowling predator-fish. The scouts reach the sunken lab and retrieve its contents.
The AI control unit still operates on the fragment, and it won't let your scouts into the locked-down section. Only the captain has the high enough clearance to bypass the lockdown.
You give the command through the comm link to the AI and use your rank to override the lockdown, allowing scouts to proceed and retrieve valuable goods.
One of the reserve reactors is a part of the fragment. Its fuel core has survived the fall and can be salvaged.
The scouts retrieve the power source from the reactor and bring to the ship.
A small fragment of the mothership looks gargantuan next to the Behemoth. It has not yet sunk beneath the waves, and you can find perhaps something of value there.

The scouts breach the fragment and report having found one of the reserve reactors, whose fuel core can still be salvaged, and the experimental lab on fire. Another section of the wreckage is a mess of fused metal, but perhaps a deep scan from a tricoder can help determine whether anything valuable and worth saving is still hidden somewhere inside.
One of the reserve reactors is a part of the fragment. Its fuel core has survived the fall and can be salvaged.
The scouts retrieve the power source from the reactor and bring it to the ship.
Equipped with portable force shields, the scouts can ignore the fire and retrieve the research from the lab.
The scouts return from the fire unscathed and with treasures of human ingenuity developed in the lab.
Provide the crew with a tricoder to help in their exploration of the wreckage.
The scouts use the tricoder to probe and detect anything undamaged behind the debris.
A familiar distress signal emanates from the island. It must belong to one of the lifepods from Zephyrus.

The scouts push forward through the island's territory, tracking down the distress signal, their eyes peeled for the lifepod's bright hull. Finally, the signal appears to be just behind the nearest hill's crest, which the scouts climb hastily, out of breath, impatient to find the survivors.      The sight of a large disc-shaped object, whose design is as deliberate as it is alien, catches the searching party off guard. And no lifepod is in view: the signal is coming from the unknown object.
Keep your distance until you can establish a remote contact

It took a surprising amount of computing resources to decipher the signal. We still aren’t sure whether we understood them or they adapted to our deciphering system.      Anyway, we managed to understand each other. The creature asks for our help in repairing the ship. First of all, they need materials.
Send a team to contact the creature personally
The creature had a translation device effective enough to provide live communication. They asked for our help in repairing their ship, mostly by providing materials.
Time to deliver the goods.
The pilot greets us, as Behemoth enters their communication range. They are happy to see us returning.
Deliver the required materials.

The pilot is grateful. They gift you a strange device; they said they’ve found it in the nearby ruins. This looks like a Primordial tech.      The pilot asks you for another favor. They need a special material. As they describe it, it looks more like a myth than real stuff. Our extraction technology wouldn’t be able to detect and refine it. Fortunately, our new friend apparently knows where we can find some.
Provide help in repairing.

Politely, they decline. You are sure they don’t want us to learn more about them.  To ease the situation, the pilot asks you for another favor. They need a special material. As they describe it, it looks more like a myth than real stuff. Our extraction technology wouldn’t be able to detect and refine it. Fortunately, our new friend apparently knows where we can find some.
Provide materials and scan the repair process
ShortDescription: Learn how the pilot repairs the ship

LongDescription: The gathered data unveils at least some of the tech the pilot uses. No doubt it is at least on the level with our, if not higher. We also detected intense data transfer, both short and long range. Let’s see if we can decipher something from it. The pilot asks you for another favor. They need a special material. As they describe it, it looks more like a myth than real stuff. Our extraction technology wouldn’t be able to detect and refine it. Fortunately, our new friend apparently knows where we can find some.
Coordinates show the Eldritium should be somewhere in these caves
We are picking lifesigns in there. Better be careful.
Warned means armed. But it doesn’t hurt to be actually armed.

The precautions weren’t in vain. The team encounters some underground predators but manages to scare them off with flares and tasers. The caves appear to be ancient ruins, abandoned centuries if not millenia ago. Eldritium here wasn’t a natural deposit but a stockpile of some long-gone facility. You pick up all you can find.
No risks taken. Send expendable machines to do the job.

The drones faced some aggressive underground creatures, clearly unhappy with the intrusion. We lost several drones before the rest managed to reach the deposits. Actually, the feedback we received shows that caves are some abandoned underground facility, and Eldritium here was stockpiled by the local dwellers. Drones grabbed what they could and retreated.
R&D is ready to start deciphering the intercepted transmissions
There’s a high risk of data corruption during the process. We should determine the priorities
Let's try to determine who the pilot contacted and why.

We couldn’t detect the receiver of the transmission, neither to fully decipher the messages. Still, we managed to determine that large data packages were containing the data on Behemoth. The Pilot gathered it and sent it to someone on the planet.
What data did the pilot gather during the repairs?

As far as the R&D can tell, the pilot scanned the Behemoth and surveyed our activities. Same as we. Was it just a curiosity, or an intentional reconnaissance? Either way, this will give us a better understanding of their communications.
The ship is repaired, and our new friend is preparing to depart
The alien is very secretive, and the farewell conversation may be very brief.
Try to keep it short, but use all the capacities available to make the conversation deep and informative

The pilot isn’t very talkative, but through the analysis we can presume that they aren’t the only one here on Keeling, and it seems there’s a permanent base of their kind somewhere. Also, the AI predicts there aren’t many of them on the planet. Their self-name is something that can be roughly translated as Luminids or Light-bringers. Sounds ominous.      As the ship leaves you scan the island gathering all that was left by the Luminid. Not much, but maybe it will help in other variations.
Try to make them stay as long as possible to gather all the available data
ShortDescription: Perform an in-depth scanning of the alien and their ship.

LongDescription: The alien we faced is, in fact, not as alien as we thought. The gathered data shows many matches with the early Earth history in the fields of alien visits to the planet. These creatures are capable of intergalactic travel and presumably have watched over us for centuries. How did they get on Keeling, and what are they searching for?      As the ship leaves you scan the island gathering all that was left by the Luminid. Not much, but maybe it will help in other variations.
Try to keep it short, but use all means to make the conversation deep and informative

The previously gathered data provided the AI with larger learning base, so we obtained more then the pilot intended to give us. They call themselves Luminids (or at least this is the closest word the AI could find to match the original meaning). They have a small outpost here, so the pilot isn’t the only Luminid here. They are interested in us, but also afraid (for some reason). And, most importantly, they came to Keeling for a reason. Perhaps the same reason we did.
The settlement spotted by Mnemosyne looks like an ordinary fishing village, but its hustle and bustle (not yet interrupted by your arrival) can easily compete with larger townlets or even cities.

This is no mere fishing village, but a trading post with a few dozen workers, their supervisors, inns, warehouses, and a pier for ships to load and unload. A three-person envoy greets your scouts with utmost courtesy, while the rest stops to gawk at your people and, even more impressive, your ship. The entire communication is conducted through gestures, as the translation devices are still processing the language, and soon it becomes clear that you are invited to barter your goods.
The local traders are clearly interested in our technologies and willing to buy even the simplest samples.

Nasobi is the name of the people on the island. While it is too soon for the translators to understand the intricacies of their culture and politics, it is clear that this outpost is a part of something bigger. Their ledgers are filled with long lists of goods flowing in and out. A maritime republic? A trading company?      More answers will surely be found, as long as the trade continues, for that seems to be the main interest of Nasobi.
The warehouses are currently filled with rare metals. In exchange, the densely furred merchants want food supplies.

The envoy representatives are also willing to part with some of their workers in exchange for certain resources.

By working together, we can learn more about Nasobi (that is the name of these people, according to the now-working, though on a limited capacity, translators).  Also, extra pairs of hands (and they have two of those) will definitely benefit the mission.
An ancient city sprawls on the island, majestic and sad, its former glory reflected in ruined buildings and echoed in neglected streets.

The city is decadent and oppressively hollow. This is what the death of a city looks like: dry canals, empty squares with roaming, wind-carried litter, and buildings that shelter mildew and decay.  But despite the appearance of absolute abandonment, the city is not as empty as one might think. Semi-transparent amphibians, frightful but curious, appear from one of the structures. They use electromagnetic waves to communicate, and your people wait for the translating devices to pick up the pattern.
We can help them with repairs. Almost everything here is withered and ruined. Any renovation will help.

The name of these people translates as Aetherids, and they prove to be open-minded and friendly. There are few of them currently in the city, as most have left to grow old, or for other reasons (the translators are fuzzy on the details).  The remaining Aetherids claim they refuse to age, whatever it means, and have decided to stay. Their petulant words are supported by their actions: playful and impulsive, they can barely sit still.
We may use their hospitality to learn more about this civilization. The scale of the city is amazing, so we definitely should learn more about its builders and the reason for their demise.

There are so few of them here, isolated and alone. Maybe we should ask them to join us? Their prowess with electric currents and electromagnetic waves can prove useful on our journey.

Out of nowhere, a group of large anthropods covered in spiky armor and armed with crude melee weaponry appears on the deck of your ship. When one of the worker drones comes into their view, they all shout their rebel yells and attack, moving rather swiftly despite their size. However, their fighting zeal helps little when the security guards join the fray: bone axes and greatswords stand no chance against firearms. As a result, a couple of anthropods are felled, many flee and jump out of the ship, and your people capture the rest as prisoners.
We need to know more about the creatures who attacked us, their motives and means. At the very least, to know what to expect.

Surprisingly enough, the prisoners are willing to cooperate and even demonstrate loyalty. Apparently, being taken as a prisoner means changing allegiance to the captor, and it's considered normal.  The name 'Crabari' is soon coined by the crew. Their self-names roughly translate as "Those who ride the sea giants." And it is not a metaphor, according to Crabari. They are nomads who travel on the backs of giant sea beasts, the hunter-gatherers of Sea. They have only recently migrated to the local waters, being as much guests here as the Behemoth and its crew.
They are savages, brutal and primitive. We must lock them up until we can kick them off the ship at the nearest island.

We've just detected half-sunken ruins of an unknown civilization. Should we send scouts to investigate?

These structures weren't flooded: they were designed to be mostly underwater. There's nobody on the upper levels, and it is hard to tell how long this place has been abandoned (if at all), but there are lots of remnants of the former dwellers.
There are plenty of items lying here and there. Some of them look like practical tools, others — like parts of the complex gadgets. And some bear ritualistic features.

The relics are not from a single culture or a single period of time. Whoever hoarded them here had a lot of time and energy to spend. A couple of relics stand out from the others. These tools weren't made for human hands, for no hands at all. Something utterly alien dwelled here.
The walls are covered with inscriptions, thousands and thousands of words (or whatever those are). We can try to scan and decipher them.

The texts here are written in several languages by different species, but they all tell similar stories. Stories about the dwellers of the deep, able to read minds and control your body. The all-knowing and ever-united, they instill fear, can kidnap or even enslave, but never start wars. Through the massive data stored here, we know a lot about the Knidaria even before encountering them.
The dark, algae-covered hallways lead deeper. But the crew, creeped out by the shadows and tomb-like silence, would dive deeper only if armed.

Our team reached the great hall, with a table in the center and a strange artifact on top of it. They also spotted a shade, hastily leaving the hall — a giant cloaked figure emitting a dim glow. They didn't chase her, but she returned in a few minutes. It was a giant cyber-implanted medusa towering above the humans, speaking directly to their heads. That's how the humans first met Knidaria.

A flying creature awkwardly lands on the deck, flops down, bleeding. Dumbfounded and in much pain, it doesn't seem to present any threat to your crew, who start to provide first aid. Then, a whole flock of these creatures appears in the sky and descends to your deck. They make angry whistling sounds too complex to be ignored: it's clearly a language! The translation is not required, though, as it soon becomes clear that they want you to stop helping the wounded creature. Instead, they gesture for you to throw the flyaway aboard.
This is an angry mob, craving to shed blood on your deck — something you simply cannot allow to pass.

The flock is infuriated. They curse in their strange ululation with the desperate intensity of someone in pain. They try to change your mind, and when you don't, they angrily leave. Your translators pick up the last phrase as something like: 'Leave it as your (pet? slave?). May this Auri suffer (flymany?)' Once recovered, the saved Auri shows far less intelligence than their kin in the flock, but they act in a friendly and helpful manner, aiding the crew with some simple tasks.
You don't know what's going on. Perhaps you're aiding a criminal. You should comply and throw the creature overboard.

The flock watches the execution from a distance. The wounded Auri (for that is how the flock calls themselves) tries to stay afloat, but weakened by the blood loss, soon stops struggling. The flock approaches the deck, leaving the symbolic gift — a jeweled headpiece.
You know too little to act rashly. Let's wait for the translators to pick up their language and try to talk it all out.

The ship's systems have detected a wide variety of valuable resources, all conveniently placed in the same corner of the island. It is highly unlikely for all these elements to have naturally come from the same source. It warrants an investigation.

As the scouts reach the supposed location of the promised resources, they find a large pyramidal mound riddled with holes and buzzing insects. It appears to be a nest, whose residents boast intimidating appendages — long stingers and impressive mandibles. Upon further examination, the scouts establish that the mound is a large pile of crates containing the various resources detected by the ship's systems. The lack of any structures or other traces of social activity around the nest hints at this being an old stash, refashioned by the insects into their home.
Put a smelly bait nearby to lure some of the insects away and leave some of the crates unattended.
The scouts hastily grab the resources from the cleared crate and retreat from the irritated insects.
Cover up some of the holes to prevent the insects from attacking you while your scouts gather the scattered resources nearby.
The scouts hastily pick up the scattered resources and flee before the angry insects can get to them .
Burn out the insects from one of the crates and collect the resources afterwards.
The scouts hastily grab the resources from the cleared crate and retreat from the irritated insects.
A shipwreck has been spotted in the vicinity. The design matches the [Species_Type]'s shipmaking traditions. The vessel has sustained substantial damage and is quickly sinking. No survivors detected.

Flying over to the shipwreck, your scouts find neither survivors nor their bodies. Not a trace, not a speck of blood. In the split cargo hold lie several human-made crates bearing Zephyrus's markings. This ship must have salvaged part of your mothership's wreckage or stumbled upon a supply beacon.      One of the ship's halves is already slipping beneath the waves. Time is running out. Which crates should your scouts save, and how?
Erect a lattice of steel supports to brace the sinking half against the Behemoth. It should buy your crew enough time to clear out this part of the cargo hold.

The support system allows your crew to safely retrieve a crate from Zephyrus packed with basic scanners and a few barrels of recently caught krill. Perhaps the ruined ship was primarily a fishing vessel.
Fabricate custom reinforcement plates and polymer seals to close the other half's fractures. Once stabilized, your crew can extract the contents of this part of the cargo hold.
The crew patches the wreck, winning a few precious minutes, and retrieves a few crates with goods. Crates from Zephyrus contain battery blocks. Locally manufactured crates have gold bars inside.
There is a large reinforced cube covered in alien writings. Too heavy to be lifted. But it appears to have a locking mechanism that your scouts can try to pick.
The crew is almost out of time and about to go down with the ship when they finally bypass the lock. Inside, they find a strange relic, whose purpose is a mystery for now.
A thick column of smoke rises from the island. A large fire, perhaps.

A fragment of Zephyrus made its way to this island. It struck a cliffside, causing an avalanche of rocks and burning metal parts to tumble down onto a small valley. In addition to pieces of Zephyrus and rock rubble, your scouts find elements of ruined structures: an outpost or a small settlement, now buried under the fallen debris.      Perhaps something valuable can be retrieved from this mess before the fire finishes its job.
By some luck, one of Zephyrus's fragments contains a mostly intact blueprinting station. Its memory bank is compromised, so it has a limited pool to draft from. To work, it must be fueled first.
The fueled device can only access and produce two building schematics. Still, better than nothing.

Another piece of Zephyrus is buried under the rocks. Carefully placed explosion charges should be the most efficient way to access the fragment. However, it could compromise the local ruins and other parts of Zephyrus.

To say the scouts were extremely lucky is to belittle just how lucky they were. The recently buried part of Zephyrus had an intact fuel container that could have exploded if the charges had been placed differently.       However, as predicted, the explosions have ruined whatever else was in the vicinity.
Try to learn more about the history behind the local ruins, now about to be erased by the fallen debris and fire.

The scouts are unable to learn anything from the uncovered ruins. Too much damage. It does not appear to have been a settlement, though: too small for that. So, probably, an outpost or a hideout.      While the investigation failed to deal with the curiosity, it was not for nothing. The scouts have retrieved several bars of Eldritium.
There is an area on this island that defies scanning by your ship's systems. A veritable blind spot. Whatever causes it warrants an investigation.

Radial support trusses and heavy conduits hold a strange Primordial cube suspended within a colossal ring-shaped structure towering in the middle of nowhere. An alarm bellows in the air.      Clusters of computers and chambers surround the ring, shooting conduits into its reinforced outer layer. When the scouts try to reach the ring, an invisible boundary overwhelms them with dizziness, nausea, and unsettling auditory hallucinations. They notice a red line on the platform, crossing which leads to a brain meltdown. While they cannot reach the ring, they notice several containers housed on separate monorails connected to the cube.      Three of the containers have glowing monitors on.
The scouts claim that this container 'requires' cultured meat, offering biochemical compounds in return. They cannot explain much else except that it is urgent.

Upon returning, the scouts display the same concussion-like symptoms: dizziness, nausea, headaches, and severe disorientation. They can vaguely describe the structure they saw, the Primordial cube, and the sound of an alarm, but when pressed for details, they fail to provide anything substantial. They cannot explain why they believed the cube was Primordial or what technology was employed in that ring-shaped installation. The one thing they do all agree on is that the whole structure inexplicably vanished in the end. They could not verify the exact time of the disappearance, but it must have happened during the takeoff.      The scouts recall an overwhelming, irresistible sense of urgency while handling automated cargo containers. They could not agree on whether the interface on the containers was in any known language, but they could understand it. There was a request and a reward. And so it happened: once loaded, the chosen container moved into the suspended cube and returned with different cargo.
